narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly drove this outcome were your LSAT score, your class ranking in the third year of law school, and your first-year class ranking. In that order of importance, each of these pushed the prediction firmly toward failure rather than success.

Your LSAT score of 19 was far below the average of 37 seen among students who were accepted, and this gap had the single largest negative impact on your chances. Your first-year and third-year decile rankings of 1.0 were also well below the averages of roughly 6.0 and 5.8 among accepted students; both placed you near the very bottom of your class and further increased the predicted risk of failing the bar.

Your low family income, undergraduate GPA of 3.0, and full-time work plans played smaller roles and did not change the overall picture.

To improve your prospects, focus on raising your LSAT score substantially through intensive preparation, as this was the most influential factor. Consider retaking key courses or seeking academic support to strengthen your class standing, then reapply once you can demonstrate clearer readiness for the bar exam.
